claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
The baseline alloy has a density of approximately 12–13 g/cm³.
The baseline alloy is brittle at room temperature, with compressive fracture strain below 5%.
Adding 0.5–2.0 at.% Al and applying solution treatment plus aging will precipitate an ordered B2 phase in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
Aging at 800–1000 °C for 10–50 hours will produce a reticulated network of coherent or semi-coherent Al-rich B2 precipitates in a disordered BCC matrix.
An inverted microstructure consisting of a continuous disordered BCC matrix and B2 precipitates can improve room-temperature strength-ductility synergy relative to a continuous B2 matrix.
The B2 phase will provide precipitation or order strengthening.
The disordered BCC matrix will retain ductility.
The reticulated B2 network will blunt, bridge, or deflect cracks and promote dislocation activity in the BCC matrix.
Cracks encountering the B2 network will be forced to deflect or require dislocation shearing of the precipitates, thereby increasing fracture strain.
Coherent interfaces will prevent premature interfacial debonding.
The intervention will raise compressive yield strength by 20–40%, from about 1000 MPa to 1300–1400 MPa.
The intervention will raise compressive fracture strain from below 5% to above 15–20%.
Adding Al will increase density by approximately 0.1–0.3 g/cm³.
The modified alloy will remain high-density because its density is dominated by Hf, Zr, Ta, and Mo.
At sufficiently high Al content, substituting low-density Al may instead slightly decrease density.
Excessive Al may produce a continuous brittle B2 matrix and reduce ductility.
Excessive aging temperature may coarsen the precipitates and cause loss of coherency.
A continuous brittle secondary-phase film at grain boundaries would be detrimental to ductility.
Room-temperature compression at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 is the proposed operating and evaluation regime.

contradictions.description: The density prediction first states that low-density Al will increase density by 0.1–0.3 g/cm³, but then allows that Al may cause a slight density decrease. No compositional or volumetric basis is given to resolve these opposing directions.
